name: Haus-Nous
summary: Haus-Nous is a website, built with Next.js, that presents a set of AI tools and business strategy frameworks. Visitors can browse a catalog of AI tools, open a detail page for each one, and look through a library of 12 strategy frameworks. There are also two screens where a user describes a business challenge and gets a simulated reply: a chat screen and a terminal-style console. The replies are described as simulated, so it is unclear whether any real AI or server sits behind them. The look is dark and techy, with a sidebar for navigation.
who_its_for: Business people and teams exploring AI tools and strategy ideas for their challenges. It may also be a demo or prototype, but the summaries do not say for certain.
how_it_runs: It runs as a Next.js website using the commands listed in package.json, and each page is a file inside the app folder. The summaries do not say where it is hosted or whether a database or outside service is used.

areas.name: (root files)
areas.summary: Settings files that set up the project: its name and run commands, the TypeScript checker, the build step for styles, the Tailwind colors and fonts, and Next.js options.
areas.why: They control how the site is built and styled, but rarely hold the content people see.
areas.debug_tips: If the site will not start or build, or colors and fonts look wrong, check package.json, tailwind.config.ts and tsconfig.json first.

areas.name: app
areas.summary: The home page, the shared outer frame that wraps every page, and the global style sheet with the dark look and moving gradient.
areas.why: This is the first thing visitors see and it sets the look for the whole site.
areas.debug_tips: If something looks off on every page, such as the background, fonts or browser tab title, look at app/layout.tsx and app/globals.css.

areas.name: components
areas.summary: Reusable visual pieces: the left sidebar navigation, an animated cat logo, and a set of line-drawing icons for tool cards.
areas.why: They are shared across pages, so one change shows up in many places.
areas.debug_tips: If the menu links, logo animation or tool card icons are wrong, check the matching file here.

areas.name: app/tools
areas.summary: The tools catalog, with search and filters by industry, category and customizability, plus a detail page for each tool chosen by its id.
areas.why: This is the main product showcase of the site.
areas.debug_tips: If a tool card is missing or a detail page shows the wrong tool, check the id handling in app/tools/[id]/page.tsx and the list in app/tools/page.tsx. Where the tool data itself lives is unclear from the summaries.

areas.name: app/chat
areas.summary: A chat screen where a user types a business challenge and gets a simulated reply with suggested tools.
areas.why: It gives visitors an interactive way to be pointed toward tools.
areas.debug_tips: Replies are simulated, so odd answers likely come from the page's own built-in logic in app/chat/page.tsx rather than a real AI.

areas.name: app/console
areas.summary: A terminal-styled screen where a user describes a strategy challenge and gets a simulated analysis.
areas.why: It offers a second, more stylized way to try the product idea.
areas.debug_tips: Check app/console/page.tsx for how the fake analysis is produced. Nothing in the summaries suggests a real backend.

areas.name: app/frameworks
areas.summary: A library page with a fixed list of 12 business strategy frameworks shown as cards that can be searched and filtered.
areas.why: It adds educational content that supports the tools.
areas.debug_tips: If a framework is missing or search misbehaves, look at app/frameworks/page.tsx, since the list is fixed there.

areas.name: lib
areas.summary: No file summaries were given for this area, so what it contains is unclear.
areas.why: Folders with this name usually hold shared helper code, but that is a guess.
areas.debug_tips: Open the folder directly to see what is inside before relying on it.

readiness.summary: The top three fixes are to add automated tests, to add CI with a documented deploy and rollback process, and to add logging plus clear error handling with input validation on the chat endpoint. Several checks (access, dependencies, data) could not be confirmed without running tools or reading the code.

checks.question: Does the app build and start with one documented command?
checks.evidence: `package.json` has standard `dev`, `build` and `start` scripts and a `package-lock.json` exists, but the README excerpt shown does not document an install and run command. Not checked: the build was not run.
checks.next_step: Add a Getting Started section to `README.md` with `npm install`, `npm run dev`, and `npm run build && npm start`.

checks.question: Are there automated tests, and do they pass?
checks.evidence: 0 test files found and `package.json` has no test script or test dependency.
checks.next_step: Add a test runner (Vitest or Jest) with a few tests for key pages and logic, plus an `npm test` script.

checks.question: When something goes wrong, does the app show a clear message instead of crashing or failing silently?
checks.evidence: Not checked: no evidence of error boundaries, `error.tsx` or API error handling was provided. No swallowed-error patterns were found, but that is not proof of clear messages.
checks.next_step: Add `app/error.tsx` and `app/not-found.tsx`, and show friendly errors in the chat UI when a request fails.

checks.question: Does it check what people type or upload before using it?
checks.evidence: Only 3 input validation matches in 2 files, so validation is minimal. No schema library such as zod is listed in the scripts and deps excerpt.
checks.next_step: Validate chat input and any API route bodies with a schema (e.g. zod) and enforce length limits.

checks.question: Are passwords and API keys kept out of the code and out of git history?
checks.evidence: No env files are tracked, `.gitignore` mentions `.env`, and 0 secret-looking strings were found in HEAD. Git history was not scanned.
checks.next_step: Run a history scan (gitleaks or trufflehog) and add a `.env.example` listing required variables.

checks.question: Can only the right people see and change things (sign-in and permissions)?
checks.evidence: Not checked: 16 auth/session/permission matches in 2 files, but their content was not shown, so it is unclear whether real sign-in or role checks exist.
checks.next_step: Review those 2 files. If the app has private data or AI usage costs, add real authentication and server-side authorization on API routes.

checks.question: Is important data backed up, and are database changes made through migrations?
checks.evidence: Not checked: no migrations folder and no database or backup configuration were seen. The app may be static and have no database.
checks.next_step: State in `README.md` whether any data is stored. If so, add migrations and a backup plan.

checks.question: Are third-party packages reasonably up to date and free of known security problems?
checks.evidence: Not checked: the dependency audit was not run. `package-lock.json` exists, which helps reproducible installs, but versions and known vulnerabilities were not assessed.
checks.next_step: Run `npm audit` and `npm outdated`, and add Dependabot or Renovate.

checks.question: If it breaks while people use it, will logs or alerts show what happened?
checks.evidence: Only 1 logging match in 1 file, and no monitoring or alerting configuration is present.
checks.next_step: Add structured server-side logging for API routes and connect an error tracker such as Sentry.

checks.question: Does it stay fast with realistic amounts of data and users?
checks.evidence: Not checked: no load or performance evidence was provided. The tool and framework catalogues look like static content, which is usually cheap to serve, but this is unverified.
checks.next_step: Run Lighthouse on key pages and confirm the chat endpoint has rate limiting and timeouts.

checks.question: Is there a written, repeatable way to deploy it and to roll back a bad release?
checks.evidence: No CI or deploy files were found and no deploy or rollback steps are documented.
checks.next_step: Add a CI workflow for lint and build, and document deploy and rollback (e.g. Vercel promote previous deployment) in `README.md`.

checks.question: Could someone new run it and understand it from the docs alone?
checks.evidence: `README.md` is the only doc. It describes the product, design and tech stack well, but the excerpt shows no setup steps, environment variables or architecture notes.
checks.next_step: Add setup, environment variable and project structure sections to `README.md`.

readiness.method: Static evidence only; tests, build and audit were not run in this pass.

debug_playbook.symptom: The site will not start or build
steps: Check that the run commands and needed libraries in package.json are present.
Look for strictness or path settings in tsconfig.json that could cause errors.
Check next.config.js for options that might be too strict.

debug_playbook.symptom: Colors, fonts or background look wrong across the whole site
steps: Confirm the style sheet is loaded in app/layout.tsx.
Check the palette and fonts in tailwind.config.ts.
Make sure postcss.config.js still runs Tailwind.

debug_playbook.symptom: A tool page shows the wrong tool or is blank
steps: Compare the id in the card link with the id the detail page looks up.
Check whether the tool exists in the data used by both pages.
Test search and filters in the catalog to see if the card is hidden.

debug_playbook.symptom: Chat or console gives strange or unhelpful answers
steps: Remember the replies are simulated, so look at how each page builds its answer.
Try different inputs to see whether the reply changes at all.
Check the console page the same way if the issue is only there.

debug_playbook.symptom: Sidebar link, logo or icon is missing or broken
steps: Check the four links in Navigation.tsx match real page addresses.
Check the logo file for its timer and hover behavior.
Check that the tool cards use the icon names defined in TechIcons.tsx.

glossary.meaning: The framework that runs this website and turns each page file into a web address.
A styling tool that lets the site use short class names for colors, spacing and fonts.
A stricter form of JavaScript that catches mistakes before the site runs.
The shared outer frame, such as styles and navigation, that every page sits inside.
A reusable piece of the screen, like the sidebar or a logo.
A made-up answer shown to look like an AI response, not necessarily from a real AI.
A build step that processes the style sheets, here to run Tailwind and Autoprefixer.
A web address such as /chat, which matches a page file in the app folder.
